newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION - Market complacent on NZ election outcome.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Market complacent on NZ election outcome.

text.p: By Matthew Goodson, economist at Garlick & Co
WELLINGTON, Sept 26 - Over the course of May and June, New Zealand financial markets talked themselves into an absolute spin on the subject of political risk.

Since then, a gradual erosion of NZ First's poll support has seen the focus turn very much back to core economic information, most of which has been favourable in terms of pointing to a future monetary easing. Thus the attitude of the market towards politics has gone full circle, with the overall view now being one of utter complacency.
In what follows, we argue that the numbers for a right-leaning coalition are by no means certain and that the risks of alternative political outcomes have not been priced into NZ financial assets.

Financial markets have taken considerable solace from the recent rise of the Christian Coalition and ACT past five percent in most polls and the strong likelihood that United will take Ohariu. However, it is not clear that a right-leaning coalition will be the result.
Many of the Christian and ACT voters would otherwise vote National and there will be a very low "wasted list vote" percentage on parties who fail to make the five percent threshold.
Thus a coalition may need up to 49 percent of the list vote to actually have a majority in Parliament. If there is an electorate seat overhang, then the requirement would move past 50 percent.
In contrast to the doubt surrounding the right-leaning coalition numbers, a grouping of Labour, NZ First and the Alliance clearly adds up.

Previously, this was dismissed as extremely unlikely given the Alliance's refusal to participate in any formal coalition structures but the recent commitment by Jim Anderton to take part in a "Clayton's coalition" has brought the left-leaning bloc right back into the picture. Similarly, the fact that Labour is slowly consolidating itself above NZ First means that such a coalition is a real possibility.
Although the precise coalition make-up is as clear as mud, one near certainty post-election is that NZ First will be in the driver's seat.

Unless the right-leaning parties sneak the thinnest of majorities, whichever way NZ First swings will prove absolutely critical. Given the public debate between Tau Henare and Winston Peters over this very issue, we could be in for a very messy coalition negotiating process.
Thus the fact that NZ First has moved back from 30 percent to around 18 percent really means nothing because in the final analysis, they are likely to hold the balance of power.
Although a lack of cross-party agreement may prevent major policy changes, one can only imagine the uncertainty that will prevail as financial markets hang on Winston Peters' every word.

It has become something of a party mantra that MMP will result in no major policy changes. At a surface glance, academic studies support this conclusion, which revolves on the key tenet that insufficient cross-party agreement is possible to make any such changes.

However, to rest on this conclusion is to totally misrepresent the argument. A left-leaning coalition could still have a considerable impact on economic policy, it's just that this impact would be larger still if FPP prevailed.
Thus while MMP will prevent the complete overthrow of the existing policy framework in the event of a left-leaning coalition, the precise outcome of the election will still matter an awful lot.
To be a devil's advocate, let's sketch a scene of the sorts of policy prognostications that markets will likely have to grapple with in the weeks following the election.

Look out for kites to be flown on subjects such as considerable fiscal policy concessions, amendments to the Employment Contracts Act in favour of collective bargaining, a capital gains tax, a higher top income tax rate, a higher
company tax rate, a move away from light-handed regulation of utilities, a wider inflation target and a further tightening of immigration criteria.

While no single one of these possible policies constitutes an abandonment of the existing framework, they collectively add up to something that financial markets would be rather less than enthused with.
Such policies would be by no means abnormal in the context of the rest of the OECD but this begs the question of why overseas investors are so heavily weighted in NZ compared to other countries.

The short term impact on these investors' perceptions of a messy coalition negotiation process and the disappearance of the multi-year free lunch on the NZ dollar (in the event of a wider inflation target) need only be imagined.
Unless the right-leaning parties gain an electoral majority, the remainder of 1996 will not be a happy time for financial markets.
Lest our views be put in the Dr Doom category, it is vital to note that our negativity is basically short term in nature.
Academic research into the determinants of economic growth (and hence earnings growth) shows that the degree of investment in physical and human capital is far more important than politics.
Politics only matters when it reaches the stage of civil war. Moreover, the inflationary implications of MMP will be relatively small given that central bank independence will likely remain.

A wider inflation target would release a veritable flood of funds out of cash and bank deposits in favour of bonds and equities, while a concomitant fall in the exchange rate would lend a major boost to earnings growth. However, these factors may not make themselves apparent for quite some time after the election.

Finally, we are not saying that any of these changes will necessarily happen or that a left-wing coalition will triumph. We simply don't know. What we are arguing is that market participants will begin to talk about such changes and that the risk of their occurrence is not currently priced into financial
markets.

Investors should not put their heads in the sand and pray that a left-leaning coalition will not occur on the basis that it is too awful to contemplate. It could easily happen and prudent investors should begin accounting for the possibility now.
(Note - The opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters).
